segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus responded by speaking to them again in parables:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The kingdom of the heavens is like a king who gave a wedding feast for his son.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He sent his slaves to summon those who had been invited to the wedding feast, but they would not come.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Again he sent other slaves, saying, ‘Tell those who have been invited: “Look, I have prepared my dinner; my bulls and fattened cattle have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding feast.”’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But they paid no attention and went off, one to his own field, another to his business,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: while the rest seized his slaves, abused them, and killed them.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The king was furious. He sent his troops, destroyed those murderers, and burned their city.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Then he said to his slaves, ‘The wedding feast is ready, but those who were invited were not worthy.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So go to where the roads lead out of the city, and invite to the wedding feast everyone you find.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And those slaves went out into the roads and gathered everyone they found, both bad and good, and the wedding feast was filled with guests.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But when the king came in to look at the guests, he saw there a man who was not dressed in wedding clothes,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and he said to him, ‘Friend, how did you get in here without wedding clothes?’ But the man was struck silent.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Then the king said to the servants, ‘Bind him hand and foot and throw him out into the darkness outside. There, there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For many are invited, but few are chosen.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the Pharisees went and made a plan to trap him in what he said.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They sent their disciples to him, together with the Herodians, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth, and that you defer to no one, for you show no partiality.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So tell us what you think: is it permitted to pay the poll tax to Caesar, or not?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus, aware of their malice, said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Why are you testing me, you hypocrites?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Show me the coin for the poll tax.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they brought him a denarius.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Whose image is this, and whose inscription?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Caesar’s.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “So give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they heard this they were amazed, and they left him and went away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On that day Sadducees came to him, saying that there is no resurrection, and they asked him a question:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Teacher, Moses said, ‘If a man dies without having children, his brother shall marry his widow and raise up offspring for his brother.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Now there were seven brothers among us. The first married and died, and having no offspring he left his wife to his brother.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: The same happened with the second and the third, down to the seventh.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Last of all, the woman died.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: In the resurrection, then, which of the seven will she be the wife of? For they all had her.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You are mistaken, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For in the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels of God in heaven.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And as for the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was said to you by God:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob’? He is not the God of the dead but of the living.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when the crowds heard this, they were astonished at his teaching.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and one of them, an expert in the Law, asked him a question to test him:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Teacher, which commandment in the Law is the greatest?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: This is the greatest and first commandment.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: A second is like it: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them a question:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What do you think about the Messiah? Whose son is he?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “David’s.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “How is it, then, that David, in the Spirit, calls him Lord, saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand until I put your enemies under your feet”’?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: If David, then, calls him Lord, how is he his son?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And no one was able to answer him a word, nor from that day did anyone dare to ask him anything more.

notes.note: The Greek is plural, reflecting a Semitic way of speaking about God's dwelling that a first-century hearer would have noticed. Most English translations flatten it to 'heaven'. The plural is kept here because it is Matthew's characteristic phrase.

The Greek word denotes a person owned by a master, not a hired employee, and 'servants' softens that for a modern reader. Many recent translations now use 'slaves'. The attendants in verse 13 are a different Greek word and are rendered 'servants'.

This is not the ordinary word for a friend but a polite form of address to someone whose name is not used, something like 'my good man'. In Matthew it is used only three times, each time to a person who is in the wrong (also 20:13 and 26:50), so it carries a note of reproach, not warmth.

The traditional rendering is 'many are called'. The Greek word is from the same verb used throughout the parable for inviting guests to the feast, and 'invited' keeps that link audible. Some modern translations do the same. Others keep 'called' because of its use elsewhere in the New Testament for God's summons.

These were evidently supporters of the family of Herod, which ruled by Rome's favor, though little else is known of them. They would have been expected to approve of paying Roman tax, while many Pharisees resented it. An answer either way could therefore be used against Jesus.

The Greek borrows the Latin word census. It refers to the head tax Rome levied on subject peoples on the basis of a census, not to taxes in general. It was a sore point in Judea, where its introduction had provoked a revolt, so the question was politically dangerous.

A denarius was a Roman silver coin, roughly a day's wage for a laborer. It carried the emperor's portrait and an inscription giving his titles, which on the common coin of the period included a claim to be son of the deified Augustus. Jesus's question in the next verse turns on that image and wording.

The questioners asked whether it was permitted to 'give' the tax. Jesus answers with a different, compound verb that normally means to pay what is owed or return what belongs to another. 'Give back' keeps that shift. 'Render' in older versions carried the same sense but is no longer heard that way.

notes.phrase: saying that there is no resurrection
notes.traditional: who say there is no resurrection
notes.note: In the text translated here the phrase has no article, so it most naturally means that the Sadducees came asserting this. Many manuscripts add the article, giving 'Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection', a description of the group. Either way the point is the same: the Sadducees denied a resurrection, and their question is meant to make the idea look absurd.

The Sadducees summarize the law of levirate marriage in Deuteronomy 25:5–6. Under it a dead man's brother married the widow, and the first son counted as the dead man's heir. The Greek verb is a technical term for marrying as a brother-in-law. The verb for 'raise up' offspring is from the same root as the word for 'resurrection'.

notes.traditional: angels in heaven; the angels of God in heaven
notes.note: The Greek edition translated here reads 'angels of God'. Some important early manuscripts lack 'of God', and several modern editions and translations follow them. The meaning is not materially affected.

The traditional 'lawyer' suggests a courtroom advocate. The word refers to a specialist in interpreting the Law of Moses, much the same as the 'scribes' elsewhere in the Gospels. Many modern translations render it this way. A few manuscripts omit the word in this verse.

The Greek word is the one traditionally rendered 'Christ'. Here it has the article and is a title under discussion, the anointed king Israel expected, not a name for Jesus. 'Messiah' conveys what a first-century Jewish hearer would have heard. Several modern translations make the same distinction in the Gospels.

notes.phrase: The Lord said to my Lord
notes.traditional: The LORD said unto my Lord
notes.note: This quotes Psalm 110:1. In the Hebrew the first 'Lord' is the divine name and the second is an ordinary word for a master or superior, but the Greek uses the same word for both. Jesus's argument assumes, as his hearers did, that David composed the psalm and that the second 'Lord' is the Messiah.
